opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more underexplored areas right now. People tend to think of RL and prompt optimization as competing approaches, like you either tune the weights or you tune the prompt. But in an environment setup they fit together pretty naturally, because the environment already gives you everything you need: a task distribution, a harness that defines how the model interacts with tools, and a reward signal that tells you whether it did the thing.

Once you have that, the harness itself becomes something you can optimize. The system prompt, the tool descriptions, how you format observations coming back, even the instructions about when to stop or ask for clarification are all parameters. They're just discrete text parameters instead of continuous weights. So you can run something like a GEPA-style loop: roll out the agent, look at the trajectories and rewards, have a model reflect on where things went wrong, propose edits to the prompt or tool specs, and keep the variants that score better. It's the same rollout-and-score infrastructure you'd use for RL. You're just pointing the optimizer at a different part of the system.

What I like about that is it's cheap and fast relative to training. You don't need a big GPU cluster to find out that your tool description is ambiguous and the model keeps calling the wrong function. A lot of agent failures are really harness failures, not capability failures. The model could do the task, but the scaffolding is confusing it. Prompt optimization is a great way to surface and fix those before you spend compute on RL.

It also works as a stepping stone. If you optimize the harness first, you get a stronger baseline policy. That matters a lot for RL, because if your model almost never succeeds you get very sparse reward and learning stalls. Getting the success rate up through better prompting means that when you do start training, there's actual signal to learn from.

The caveat is overfitting. If you optimize a prompt really hard against a small eval set, you can end up with something brittle and weirdly specific. So you want held-out tasks, and you want to treat the harness like any other learned artifact: version it, evaluate it properly, and don't assume an improvement transfers to a different model. A prompt tuned for one model can be actively worse for another.

Longer term, I think the line between "harness" and "model" gets blurry. You'll co-optimize them: tune the scaffold, train the model inside it, re-tune the scaffold for the new model, and iterate. Environments are the natural unit for that because they package the task, the interface, and the evaluation together.

r001.rationale: It says the harness can be optimized and names individual targets: the system prompt, tool descriptions, observation formatting, and instructions about stopping or asking for clarification.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that the harness is really just another thing you can optimize, and prompt optimization is kind of the cheapest, most accessible lever you have before you ever touch the weights.

When we build environments at Prime Intellect, we're defining this loop: the model gets a system prompt, some tools, some observation format, and it produces actions until it hits a terminal state and gets a reward. People tend to treat everything except the model as fixed scaffolding. But the system prompt, the tool descriptions, the way you render the environment state back to the model, the error messages you feed back when a tool call fails, those are all free parameters. And they matter a lot. We've seen cases where a bad tool description costs you more than a mediocre checkpoint does.

So the nice thing is, once you have a verifiable reward, you can run the exact same optimization loop you'd run for RL, but over the prompt and harness instead of the parameters. You sample a bunch of rollouts, you score them, and then you have something, could be a human, could be another model, could be a DSPy-style optimizer, look at the failures and propose edits to the instructions or the tool specs. Then you re-evaluate. It's basically a search over harness configurations with the environment as the objective function.

The part I find most interesting is doing this before and alongside RL rather than instead of it. If you start RL on a harness with a garbage prompt, the model has to spend a bunch of its learning budget just figuring out what you meant, and that shows up as a slow, noisy early phase. If you prompt-optimize first, you get a much stronger starting policy, which means more of your rollouts are in the interesting regime where the model is actually succeeding sometimes, and that's where RL signal comes from. And then there's a feedback effect in the other direction too: after you've trained a model, the optimal prompt for it shifts, so you can go back and re-optimize the harness for the new checkpoint. The two kind of co-evolve.

There are a couple of things to be careful about, though. One is that prompt optimization overfits really easily. If your eval set is small, you'll find a prompt that games it, and it won't transfer. So you want held-out tasks, same as you'd want for training. The other is that you want to optimize the harness for things that are genuinely about the interface, like clarity of tool semantics or output formatting, and leave the stuff that's really about capability to the weights. If you find yourself writing a three-page system prompt that walks the model through the reasoning step by step, that's usually a sign you should be training on it, not prompting it.

The ideal in my head is that the environment author gives you a reward and a rough sketch of the harness, and then the optimization process, both prompt-level and weight-level, fills in the rest. We're not fully there, but it's a lot closer than it was a year ago.

r001.rationale: The response identifies the system prompt, tool descriptions, environment-state rendering, and tool-failure messages as harness components that can be optimized.

astra-6.text:
I think you can treat a lot of the harness as something to optimize, rather than something you write once and leave fixed. There’s the system prompt, but also the tool descriptions, the instructions you give when a tool fails, and how you summarize context as the trajectory gets longer. All of those can affect how the agent behaves.

If you have environments where you can measure success, you can run the agent, look at where it fails, propose changes to those parts of the harness, and evaluate them on another set of tasks. So you’re using feedback from the whole trajectory to improve the instructions the agent operates under.

The thing I’d be careful about is overfitting. It’s pretty easy to produce a prompt that fixes the handful of failures you just looked at. The interesting question is whether that change helps on new tasks, too. I’d want held-out evaluations and multiple runs before deciding that a harness change is actually an improvement.

r001.rationale: The response identifies the system prompt, tool descriptions, tool-failure instructions, and context summaries as harness components that can be changed and optimized.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the harness as part of what you’re optimizing. An agent has a system prompt, tool descriptions, instructions about how to use those tools, and potentially prompts for things like summarizing its context. Those are all places where prompt optimization can help.

The way you’d do it is run the agent on a set of tasks in the environment, measure whether it succeeds, and use that feedback to propose changes to the prompts. You might discover that a clearer tool description helps more than another paragraph of general advice in the system prompt.

The important thing is to evaluate those changes on held-out tasks. It’s very easy to optimize a prompt that gets better at the particular examples you’ve been testing without making the agent more capable generally. But if you have a reliable reward signal and a reasonably representative task distribution, you can treat a lot of the harness as something you improve empirically, rather than something you have to get right by hand.

r001.rationale: The response identifies system prompts, tool descriptions, tool-use instructions, and context-summarization prompts as harness components that prompt optimization can improve.
